title: A Watchman Sent to Stubborn Exiles
overview: Ezekiel takes God's message deep inside himself, is sent to his fellow exiles who will resist it, and is made responsible for warning them.

parts.label: Eating the scroll (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The scroll from the previous chapter was full of mourning and woe, and eating it pictures Ezekiel taking God's message completely into himself before speaking it. It tastes sweet, which many read as the joy of serving God even when the message itself is grim; the bitterness comes later in verse 14.

parts.label: Sent to his own people (vv. 4-11)
parts.note: Ezekiel is not sent to foreigners he cannot understand, and God says such people would have listened more readily than Israel will. God promises to make his forehead harder than flint, meaning a resolve as stubborn as their resistance, and he must speak whether they listen or not.

parts.label: Carried to the exiles (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: As the vision lifts, Ezekiel hears the rumbling wings and wheels of the living creatures from chapter 1, then finds himself in a settlement of deported Israelites beside the river in Babylonia where that first vision happened. He sits there stunned for seven days, the customary length of mourning, sharing their grief before he says a word.

parts.label: Made a watchman (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: Like a lookout on a city wall who must sound the alarm, Ezekiel is responsible for warning people; if he stays silent he shares the blame, but if he warns them he has done his part, whatever they choose. The line about God putting a stumbling block before someone is hard, and interpreters differ on whether it means God lets a person fall further into wrong or brings ruin on them as a consequence.

parts.label: Silenced and shut in (vv. 22-27)
parts.note: After seeing God's glory again on the plain, Ezekiel is told to stay in his house, unable to speak except when God gives him a message. Scholars are unsure whether the ropes and silence were literal or a picture of his situation, and many connect this silence to its ending when news of Jerusalem's fall arrives in chapter 33.

think: Have you ever felt responsible to warn someone about something, and how did you weigh speaking up against knowing they might not listen?
